chapter: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
title: The Biggest Show of 1952 with Nat Cole, Stan Kenton and Sarah Vaughan
summary: Touring with Cole's trio and Kenton's five-section band, he meets Kenton sidemen like Stan Levey and Conte Candoli.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: In the fall of 1952, there was a show that had gone out the year before, and it was called The Biggest Show of 1951. That show featured Duke Ellington's band, Sarah Vaughan, George Kirby, an act called Stump and Stumpy, Peg Leg Bates, a lot of other people that I don't remember -- but that show had gone out in 1951. And in 1952, I guess due to the success of the 1951 show, it was decided that they would do it again. Oh, the other person, the main attraction on the show was Nat King Cole.

So they decided to do the show again and call it The Biggest Show of 1952. This show featured the Nat King Cole Trio as the headliner, and then they had Stan Kenton's band, Sarah Vaughan, George Kirby, Peg Leg Bates, Stump and Stumpy, and a few other personalities that doesn't come to mind immediately.
But that turned out to be a very successful tour, and I met a lot of musicians on there, particularly from the Stan Kenton band. Guys like Lee Konitz...
Lou Levy... No, not Lou Levy, I'm sorry. Lou Levy was a
No. Because Stan Kenton was the pianist!
Was Zoot in the band at that time?
No. The drummer was Levey... Stan Levey! Stan Levey was the drummer. Conte Candoli.
Maynard Ferguson. Richie Kamuca, a tenor saxophone player -- I think he passed away recently. A trombone player...

Rossolini (sic) -- Frank Rossolini [ROSSOLINO]. Stan Kenton had quite a band then, with a lot of musicians. As a matter of fact, he had five saxophones, five trombones, five trumpets, and four in the rhythm section. I think it was the best band that I have ever heard of Stan Kenton's.

Anyway, along with, as I said before, the Nat King Cole Trio, which at that particular time the bassist was Joe Comfort and the guitar player was John Collins, a very fine guitarist and a long-time friend. They made up the Nat King Cole Trio. Of course, there was John (sic: GEORGE) Kirby, Peg Leg Bates. It just made for a very happy situation. That
whole year of 1952 with Sarah Vaughan was just highlighted with things that were very good musically, including the money was pretty good.
